posts.title: A DNA region is not automatically a gene
posts.articleTitle: ADHD and genes: what the evidence shows
posts.learningPoint: Understand the gap between finding an associated region and identifying a causal gene.
posts.provenanceNote: author-proposed; adapted from the listed published sections, not verbatim quotations

slides.heading: What was found?
slides.body: A genome-wide association study looks for DNA variants associated with a trait across groups of people. An associated region is often called a locus.
slides.sourceSection: The deeper layer; Common locus to effector gene evidence
slides.passageRef: Author-proposed adaptation, not a quotation. Origins: PROP-0074, PROP-0080.

links.label: Demontis et al. 2023 — ADHD genome-wide analyses
links.detail: Abstract; DOI 10.1038/s41588-022-01285-8. Population associations and functional annotation; no individual causal or medication prediction.

slides.heading: Which gene matters?
slides.body: A locus can contain several candidate variants and genes. The closest gene is a clue, not an automatic answer; functional evidence helps investigate which genes may be involved.
slides.sourceSection: The deeper layer; Common locus to effector gene evidence
slides.passageRef: Author-proposed adaptation, not a quotation. Origins: PROP-0074, PROP-0080.

links.label: Demontis et al. 2023 — ADHD genome-wide analyses
links.detail: Abstract; DOI 10.1038/s41588-022-01285-8. Population associations and functional annotation; no individual causal or medication prediction.

slides.heading: What does it tell one person?
slides.body: A population association does not, by itself, identify the cause of one person’s ADHD or select their medicine.
slides.sourceSection: The deeper layer; Common locus to effector gene evidence
slides.passageRef: Author-proposed adaptation, not a quotation. Origins: PROP-0074, PROP-0080.
